summary: An index-style memo that summarizes the RFCs numbered 1200 through 1299, listing each one with its title and basic details. It is useful as a quick guide to that block of the series.

plainLanguage.summary: A table of contents for one hundred RFC documents. It lists each one with a short note so you can find the one you want.

subtitle: A catalog of 100 RFCs covering the Internet protocols from 1991-1992

tldr.problem: The RFC series had grown to over 1,200 documents by 1997, making it hard for readers to find and understand specific protocol specifications.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC summarizes the 100 documents in the 1200-1299 range, providing the title, author, date, and a one-paragraph description of each RFC's purpose and status.
tldr.outcome: Serves as an index to a block of the RFC series covering routing, network management, DNS/directory services, and infrastructure protocols published around 1991-1992.

today: RFC 1299 is an Informational RFC that serves as a historical index to a block of the RFC series. While the specific RFCs it summarizes are now over 30 years old, the document itself remains useful as a snapshot of Internet standardization work from the early 1990s.

sections.title: Finding Your Way Through 100 RFCs
sections.content:
By 1997, the RFC series had grown to nearly 1,300 documents. For engineers looking for a specific protocol or wanting to understand what work was being standardized, browsing through hundreds of titles was daunting. This RFC solves that problem for one slice of the series: it provides a catalog of RFCs 1200 through 1299, each with a brief summary explaining what it specifies and whether it is on the standards track.

The RFCs in this range were published between August 1991 and January 1997, a period when the Internet was still consolidating core protocols and management infrastructure. Many of the RFCs documented here are now Internet Standards; others are Informational (background or historical documents), Experimental (techniques not yet standardized), or have become obsolete as protocols evolved.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a guide to 100 technical documents. For each one, it says what it is about and whether it is an official standard or just information.

sections.title: Standards Track versus Informational RFCs
sections.content:
The RFCs in this range have different statuses. Many are marked [STANDARDS-TRACK], meaning they are part of the formal Internet standardization process. Some are informational, providing background, analysis, or guidance without specifying a standard (examples include internet growth statistics, security guidelines, and RFC summaries like this one). A few are Experimental, defining techniques not yet ready for standardization. The status matters: standards-track RFCs define what implementations should do, while informational RFCs help engineers understand the landscape.

The note at the beginning of RFC 1299 cautions that the standards status of these RFCs may have changed since publication, so readers should consult the latest 'Internet Official Protocol Standards' document for current status. But the catalog gives a snapshot of what was being standardized in 1991-1992: an era focused on routing (BGP, OSPF), network management (SNMP, MIBs), and directory services (X.500).
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these RFCs are official standards (the ones marked [STANDARDS-TRACK]), others are just reference material. The standards are what you have to follow; the others are helpful background.

sections.title: Network Management and Monitoring
sections.content:
A major theme in this block of RFCs is network management and monitoring: how operators observe what is happening on the network and configure devices. The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and its Management Information Base (MIB) form the core. Multiple RFCs define MIBs for different technologies: Ethernet-like interfaces (1284), FDDI (1285), bridges (1286), token rings (1231), token buses (1230), and DECnet (1289). Other management RFCs cover SNMP over alternative transports (OSI, IPX, UDP), alert handling, and remote network monitoring.

This period saw SNMP consolidating its position as the dominant network management protocol. The MIB RFCs were essential reading for anyone building network devices or management tools, as they defined the standard objects that management stations could query to learn about device configuration and performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Many RFCs here are about how network managers monitor and control equipment using SNMP: special definitions for Ethernet, fiber, bridges, and other network hardware.

sections.title: Routing and Core Infrastructure Protocols
sections.content:
Another major thread is routing and core infrastructure. The Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) routing protocol appears across multiple RFCs: version 2 of the protocol itself (1247), its MIB (1248, 1253), analysis and experience reports (1245, 1246). The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) for inter-domain routing is also covered: BGP-3 (1267), analysis (1265), experience report (1266), and application guidelines (1268). RFC 1264 standardizes procedures for routing protocol standardization itself.

Additional infrastructure protocols include improvements to the Internet Protocol itself (extensions for TCP, alternatives to IP for specialized networks), DNS and directory services (X.500, naming schemes), and encapsulation techniques for carrying one protocol inside another (IPX over IP, OSI services over UDP, AppleTalk encapsulation). These RFCs document the groundwork for scaling the Internet to new sizes and connecting it to other network types.
sections.plainLanguage: This section covers the core routing and forwarding protocols: how routers decide where to send packets. OSPF and BGP are the main routing protocols documented here.

sections.title: Mail, Services, and Infrastructure
sections.content:
Beyond routing and management, the RFCs cover mail protocols (POP version 3 for accessing remote mailboxes, SNMP encapsulation over mail systems), information services (directory protocols like X.500, the Finger protocol for user information, measurement and accounting), and infrastructure planning. RFC 1281 provides guidelines for secure Internet operation; RFC 1287 discusses future Internet architecture; RFC 1272 addresses Internet accounting and cost allocation.

Two distinctive RFCs provide a flavor of the era: RFC 1217 is a humorous memo from the 'Consortium for Slow Commotion Research' commenting on network economics, and RFC 1290 discusses interesting information repositories and resources ('gold nuggets') available on the network. RFC 1251 provides biographical information about Internet leadership (IAB, IESG, IRTF), and RFC 1244 is an early guide to Internet security for users.
sections.plainLanguage: These RFCs cover mail protocols, information services like directories and user lookups, and big-picture topics like Internet security, future directions, and how to pay for network operations.

sections.title: Legacy and Evolution
sections.content:
Many RFCs in the 1200-1299 range are now historical or obsolete, having been superseded by newer protocols. For example, earlier versions of OSPF and BGP have been replaced by newer versions with additional capabilities. Some experimental techniques (like DIXIE for directory access, various encapsulation methods) did not see widespread adoption. Others, like SNMP and the MIBs, remain foundational to network management today, though the protocols have been extended significantly.

This summary RFC (1299) itself has been succeeded by later summaries (RFC 2100 covers 2000-2099, for instance). Reading it provides a window into what the Internet engineering community was prioritizing in 1991-1992: standardizing core protocols, building management infrastructure, and preparing for growth from thousands to millions of hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these RFCs are no longer used (they were replaced by better versions), but others like SNMP are still important today. The whole collection shows what engineers thought was important in 1991.

references.text: Kennedy, M., "Request for Comments Summary: RFC Numbers 1200-1299", RFC 1299, ISI, January 1997.
